apps.name: Skate 3
apps.subtitle: Build the Skate 3 recompilation for iOS from your own disc image. Or ipa Ships no game code
apps.localizedDescription:
skate3-ios-setup:

Build the Skate 3 recompilation for iOS from your own disc image, on your own Mac, signed with your own Apple ID, installed on your own iPhone.

Runs at a locked 60fps on an iPhone 13 mini (A15): median frame 16.7ms against a 16.67ms budget, 95th percentile 16.8-17.8ms. Anything newer has more headroom than that.

Step 3 is the whole thing: it checks your tools, extracts your disc image, recompiles it, builds the app, signs it with your Apple ID, and installs it on your phone.

--recurse-submodules matters - the runtime lives in a submodule and the build will not configure without it. If you already cloned without it, run git submodule update --init --recursive inside skate3recomp-dev.

versions.localizedDescription:
Skate 3 on iOS, v2.6.0.

You must supply the game. This app contains no game content. See the setup instructions.

The completion-screen slowdown:

Mission completion and replay screens crawled, and a long session decayed toward single digits and then died with no crash report.

Finished graphics work is destroyed a little at a time so no single frame stalls. Past a threshold that limit is supposed to come off entirely and let the backlog clear. The clock came off; a cap of 256 objects per frame did not. Once a screen produced them faster than that, the backlog could only grow, every frame paid to work against a longer one, and the heap grew until iOS killed the app.

Measured on an iPhone 13 mini: a backlog of 18,000 falling by exactly 255 a frame for seventy frames at 5-36ms each, and one of those cleanups finishing its 255 objects in 508 microseconds before stopping anyway. It is now one limit instead of two - a 50ms ceiling with no object cap - so the backlog actually clears.

Quitting to the home screen after switching away:

Switching to another app and back could end the game with "Graphics device lost".

iOS refuses GPU work to an app in the background, and those refusals keep arriving for a few milliseconds after it returns. They were charged to a budget meant to absorb one occasional error every few seconds: eight arrived inside 20 milliseconds, and the ninth was treated as a real hardware failure. Failures caused by backgrounding are now recognised as such, within a bounded window so a genuinely lost device is still reported rather than hidden behind a frozen screen.

Installing the game without the file picker:

Under TrollStore or on a jailbreak, the system file picker cannot hand the app a file, and the picker was the only way to select a disc image. LiveContainer worked only because it ships its own replacement.

Drop your disc image into the Skate 3 folder in Files and it is found automatically, with no picker involved. Every candidate is verified as a real Xbox 360 disc before it is used. The picker remains available for iCloud Drive and USB storage.

An extracted disc copied across as a folder is also accepted now. Previously default.xex one level down read as "game files not found".

Also:

• Texture and mesh budgets are back to the values 2.5.0 shipped.
• The frame-time log names what the cleanup freed and which limit stopped it.

Requires iOS 16 and a 6-core device. Every iPhone that runs iOS 16 qualifies; older iPads (A9/A9X/A10/A10X) do not.

This build slows down on mission completion and replay screens, and a long session decays toward single-digit frame rates. Use the latest release.

Skate 3 for iOS — v2.5.0:

Hey — this one's a big catch-up. The last public release was v2.4.0, and everything from 2.4.1 through 2.4.7 got built and then never actually shipped, so all of it lands here at once along with the new stuff.

Install it with AltStore or SideStore. The .ipa doesn't contain the game — you bring your own copy of Skate 3 and it walks you through installing it the first time you launch.

The headline: the game used to measure itself while you played, and now it doesn't. Every build up to this point shipped with the performance tools running — a frame-timing summary, a present-cadence tracker, and a ten-clock breakdown of literally every frame that went to the screen. The lines they wrote to the log were cheap. The bookkeeping behind them ran on every single frame whether anything got printed or not, and everybody paid for it just to play the game. That's all off now.

It didn't get deleted, though — that detail is what makes a bug report useful. It moved behind a Diagnostics switch in Settings → System. If something goes wrong and someone asks you for a log, flip it on, play until it happens again, and send the log. No special build, no config files to hand-edit.

The settings menu asks before it closes the game now. On iOS, applying a setting that needs a restart means quitting — that's genuinely the only way some of them can take effect — and it used to just do it, instantly, the moment you picked it. Worse, it was also wired to a bare button on a controller, so one stray press and your session was gone. It asks now, and "Keep Playing" is the option your thumb lands on by default.

And the buttons are actually sized for fingers. Those little circles either side of each setting were built for a mouse pointer. On a phone they worked out to about two millimetres across — roughly a third of what a touch target is supposed to be — and the invisible margin around them didn't scale at all. They are more than twice the size now, with a proper margin, and the rows and category buttons grew to match.

A Potato preset, under Settings → Video → Preset, sitting below Performance. It gives the picture up rather than trimming it: no shadows at all, no ambient occlusion, bloom or sun shafts, and half the draw distance. For older phones, or for anyone who just wants every frame the hardware can produce.

Half draw distance is selectable now. The Draw Distance setting used to bottom out at "Original" — it'll go to "Half" now, which draws less of the world than the Xbox 360 itself did. On a phone this is the setting with the most room behind it, because the emulated CPU is what issues all the draw calls, so cutting them lands on emulation rather than on the GPU.

Logs got a lot quieter. The content scan used to fire off about fifty warnings every boot about files that were completely fine, which buried anything that actually mattered. A log now leads with the build version and reports real problems.

Everything from the releases that never went out:

Frame rate.

• iPhones with ProMotion displays (13 Pro and newer) were running the entire game at 30 fps. That's fixed — they run at 60 now. Touching the screen also halved the frame rate on those phones, which is fixed too.
• Every iPhone was running at half the frame rate it should have been. The graphics layer was encoding each frame's work inline while it submitted it, which serialised two things that are supposed to overlap. Measured on a real device: 30 fps to 60.

Freezes and crashes.

• The game could go permanently black while the audio just kept playing. One transient graphics error latched a flag that nothing ever cleared, and every frame after that was silently thrown away for the rest of the session.
• A startup freeze where the game booted, showed nothing, and never actually ran.
• iOS takes GPU access away when an app goes to the background. The game read that as "the graphics device died" and ended the session instead of just waiting to come back.
• Crash reports now name the exact build that wrote them, so a report from a stranger can be matched to a version.

Settings.

• They save when you close the menu, and again shortly after you change something — instead of only on a clean exit.
• The settings list scrolls by touch. It used to need a gamepad, which quietly hid everything below the fold, including the FPS counter.

What you need to run it:

An iPhone works. Some older iPads don't.

Skate 3 ran on an Xbox 360, which had six hardware threads, and the emulator maps the game's threads onto your device's CPU cores one-to-one. That needs a 6-core CPU. With fewer, the game's threads pile up on top of each other and the whole thing falls apart — measured on a 2-core iPad Pro, that's 16 fps and single locks held for sixteen seconds at a stretch.

Every iPhone that can run iOS 16 has six cores, so all supported iPhones are fine. The ones that aren't are the older iPads — anything with an A9, A9X, A10 or A10X chip (iPad Pro 1st and 2nd gen, iPad 5th–7th gen). iPadOS says they're supported and they'll install, but they don't have the cores and there is no setting that fixes that. Newer iPads with an A12X/A12Z or an M-series chip have eight cores and are fine.

Worth knowing:

The frame rate is capped at 60 by default. You can pick higher caps under Settings → Video → Framerate Cap and they work, but 120 hasn't been properly checked for physics behaviour or for how it holds up once the phone warms up, so treat those as experimental rather than a recommendation.

Also: turning quality settings down doesn't always buy you frames. On newer iPhones the GPU is idle most of each frame and the real limit is emulation, which no quality slider touches. Draw Distance is the one that reaches it.

config menu, more control options, and setup that explains itself.

Runs at a locked 60fps on an iPhone 13 mini (A15). Median frame 16.7ms against a 16.67ms budget, 95th percentile 16.8–17.8ms. so it is a real 60, not an average with dips hiding inside it. Anything newer than an A15 has more headroom than that. 70 fps uncapped in career mode and 90 fps in custom maps.

Press start and select together to get into config menu.

Installing:

1. Install the app. Download skate3.ipa below and sideload it with [Live Container] AltStore, SideStore or Sideloadly. Each re-signs it with your own Apple ID as it installs — the file here is deliberately unsigned. On a free Apple ID the app stops opening after 7 days and needs refreshing; a paid developer account lasts a year.

2. Add your own copy of the game. The app ships with no game content and will not start without it. Connect your iPhone to a computer, open Finder → your iPhone → Files → Skate 3 (on Windows, iTunes → File Sharing), and drop in a game folder containing your disc files. A full disc image is around 6 GB, so give it a few minutes.

3. Add Title Update 3. The game needs the free update EA published on Xbox Live; it is not on the disc, and the game will not run without it. iOS apps can't download it themselves, so fetch it on a computer:

Download Title Update 3 — about 1.7 MB, from the Xbox Unity archive. The file is named TU_12K2276_000000C000000.00000000000O3.

Copy it into Files → On My iPhone → Skate 3, the same way you staged the disc, then point the installer at it. It is checked against a known SHA-256 before use, so a truncated download is caught immediately rather than crashing later.

Setup now walks you through steps 2 and 3 on-screen, and no longer offers a Download button on iOS that could never have worked. That was the part nobody could get past: a 6 GB disc image cannot be picked out of the Files app if it was never copied to the phone in the first place, and the old screen just said "Select ISO" without saying how.

Requires iOS 16.0 or later. Controllers pair automatically; touch controls appear when none is attached.

New in this release:

Press Start + Select together to open the performance menu. It shows what the game is actually doing — frame rate, frame time, how long each frame spends waiting on the GPU — and then says in one line what is holding it back: the frame cap, the graphics card, or the emulation itself. That last line is the useful one. Turning quality settings down only buys you frames while it says the graphics card; if it says emulation, you are switching things off for nothing. Every quality setting worth changing sits on the same page under the readout, so you can change one and watch the number move.

More control options. Vibration strength, so you can soften the constant road buzz without losing the bails. Stick and trigger deadzones, for a worn controller that drifts on its own. Invert camera Y, and swap sticks. Each of the three shortcuts — settings, performance, level picker — can be rebound. Everything defaults to exactly what the console did, so if you change nothing, nothing changes.

This contains no game content, and never downloads any. You supply your own copy.

Spark is an independent utility for organizing and launching Ren'Py visual novels. It is not affiliated with or supported by the official Ren'Py project. For any issues with this app, please contact Spark support, not the Ren'Py team.

Launch and Play Your Novels with Ease Import and start your favorite Ren'Py visual novels directly in Spark. Once added, your titles are ready to launch with a tap, so you can focus on reading and playing instead of manual setup.

Tailored Compatibility for Each Novel Choose from multiple Ren'Py engine versions to match your novel and improve stability: 8.x: 8.5.2, 8.5.0, 8.4.1, 8.3.7, 8.3.4, 8.2.3, 8.1.3, 8.0.3 7.x: 7.8.8, 7.8.4, 7.7.3, 7.6.3, 7.5.3, 7.4.11.

apps.name: Aurora
apps.subtitle: Play RPG Maker games on your iPhone and iPad — XP, VX, VX Ace, MV, and MZ, with multiplayer, overlays, upscaling, and full save management
apps.localizedDescription:
Aurora:

Play RPG Maker games on your iPhone and iPad — XP, VX, VX Ace, MV, and MZ, with multiplayer, overlays, upscaling, and full save management.

Aurora brings the full RPG Maker experience to your iPhone and iPad with powerful tools built for mobile.

⚙️ Multi-Engine Support:

RPG Maker XP, VX, and VX Ace run natively on the Aurora Engine. MV and MZ run through Aurora's built-in web engine.

🌐 Aurora Link Multiplayer:

See other players in the overworld, chat, trade, and battle in PE games — nearby, online, or in always-on Realms.

🎛️ Overlays & Upscaling:

Quick menu, fast-forward, screenshots, and button mapping in-game. Sharpen and upscale with FSR, xBRZ, and shader presets.

🎮 Controller Support:

Play with MFi game controllers, PS4/PS5, Xbox, and other Bluetooth controllers — or the customizable touch layout editor.

apps.name: Empo
apps.subtitle: Run RPG Maker games on iPhone and iPad
apps.localizedDescription:
Empo is a game launcher for iPhone and iPad. It runs RPG Maker XP, VX, and VX Ace games, and Pokemon Essentials games. Inside, it uses mkxp-z-apple-mobile, an iOS fork of the mkxp-z engine.

The name's from emporos, ancient Greek for a traveler riding on someone else's ship.

What's new::

• Enjoy Picture in Picture, playback speeds from 0.5x to 2x, audio and subtitle track selection, precise seeking, and system media controls.
• Take playback to a bigger screen with AirPlay or a compatible player discovered on your local network.

• Select and share multiple completed files or entire folders in one go.

Improvements::

• Refreshed the interface for iOS 26, with Liquid Glass styling, cleaner dialogs, and more polished navigation.

• Improved media previewing so iTorrent can offer the best available player for each file.

• Expanded and refined translations across all supported languages.

Fixes::

• Fixed cases where magnet links could be saved incorrectly.
• Fixed a startup race condition that could interfere with launching the app or completing initial setup.
• Fixed toolbars and navigation behaving incorrectly in iPad split-screen mode.

• Fixed torrent details sometimes getting stuck in a continuous update loop.

What’s new:

• Import/Export of RSS channels.

Improvements:

• Files thumbnails now looks properly.
• Minor UI changes.

Fixes:

What’s new:

• iOS 26 Support, iTorrent fully adopted new Liquid Glass design.
• LibTorrent updated to version 2.0.11.
• On first launch, app will ask if you'd like to use Cellular connection, instead of disabling it by default.
• Added German localization.
